lesson.title: The Perfect Tense
lesson.subtitle: ik heb gewerkt, ik ben gekomen — hebben or zijn plus the ge- participle

hook.title: Have or Be, Plus Ge-
hook.content: The Dutch perfect is two pieces: a helper (hebben or zijn) and a participle. Ik heb gewerkt, ik ben gekomen, zij is gegaan. English has the same have/be split in 'I have worked' and 'I have come'.

pattern.title: Choose the helper, build the participle
pattern.content: Most verbs take hebben: ik heb gewerkt, hij heeft koffie gemaakt. Verbs of motion or change take zijn: ik ben gekomen, zij is gegaan. The participle usually begins with ge- and ends in -t or -en.
pattern.linguist_note: The perfect is a Germanic construction: a have/be auxiliary plus a past participle. English and Dutch divide the helpers along similar lines.
pattern.trap_note: Do not use hebben with gaan or komen: it is ik ben gegaan, ik ben gekomen. The helper follows the verb's meaning, not the speaker's choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The Perfect Tense):
exercises.target_answer: hebben, zijn, werken, komen, gaan, maken
exercises.meaning: to have, to be, to work, to come, to go, to make
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The Perfect Tense": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik heb gewerkt.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The Perfect Tense”.

cues: The pattern: Choose the helper, build the participle
exercises.explanation: “Wij zijn gekomen.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Choose the helper, build the participle.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not use hebben with gaan or komen: it is ik ben gegaan, ik ben gekomen. The helper follows the verb's meaning, not the speaker's choice.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Zij is gegaan.” is word-for-word “She is gone.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Choose the helper, build the participle.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: He has made coffee.
exercises.explanation: “Hij heeft koffie gemaakt.” reuses only material taught in “The Perfect Tense” — Choose the helper, build the participle.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Hij heeft koffie gemaakt.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Choose the helper, build the participle.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I have stayed home.”
twist.explanation: Blijven takes zijn, and the participle is gebleven.

foreshadow.line: The perfect will return when the modal perfect needs two infinitives. For now, the helper and participle are enough.

summary.outcome: Form the perfect with hebben or zijn and the ge- participle.
summary.takeaway: The perfect is a helper plus a participle; the helper is chosen by the verb's meaning.

hebben.etymology_derivation: English have and Dutch hebben descend from the same verb; the b is preserved.

zijn.etymology_derivation: The being verb is irregular in every Germanic language; English is and Dutch is are the same old root.

werken.etymology_derivation: English work and Dutch werken are the same verb.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

gaan.etymology_derivation: The same verb as English go, with the old g still pronounced.

maken.etymology_derivation: English make and Dutch maken are the same verb; German shifted k to ch in machen.
